title: A New Ice Age Was Beginning. Then Humans Started Burning Fossil Fuels
gist: A new Science study led by Nicolás Young of Columbia's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory uses beryllium-10 exposure dating and buried mosses to reconstruct the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island. The ice cap, a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began re-growing about 2,000 years ago, possibly the start of a new glaciation. Since the 1960s it has reversed as carbon emissions rose, with edges retreating about 4 m a year since the 1980s. The findings suggest fossil-fuel burning may have halted the next ice age.

insights.claim: A study published in Science suggests that burning fossil fuels may have stopped Earth from entering another ice age. The Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island grew for a few thousand years before rapidly reversing starting in the 1960s as carbon pollution increased.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: This is new evidence of how strongly human emissions have overridden natural climate cycles, and it strengthens the scientific case behind decarbonization policy.

insights.claim: The Barnes Ice Cap, which covers an area the size of Delaware, is a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. Beryllium-10 exposure dating shows it first reached its modern size about 3,600 years ago, and dead mosses preserved under the bedrock-frozen ice show it began re-growing about 2,000 years ago.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The method gives new proxy data for paleoclimate models used in climate-risk projections.

insights.claim: Ice ages follow natural Milankovitch cycles in Earth's rotation and orbit. The Barnes Ice Cap's regrowth about 2,000 years ago may have marked the start of another glaciation period.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: This sets the natural climate baseline against which human-caused warming is measured.
insights.locator: The planet regularly goes through phases

insights.claim: Dartmouth's Meredith Kelly praises the study's data but wants comparisons with other sites worldwide before concluding how Earth was moving into glaciation. The exact mechanisms that start ice growth still need more research.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kelly
insights.so_what: The single-site evidence carries uncertainty, so conclusions are provisional until other sites replicate them.
insights.locator: Meredith Kelly, a professor of earth sciences at Dartmouth

insights.claim: Nicolás Young says the study helps show that scientists at an early-1970s Brown University meeting were right about a pending glaciation. That meeting sent a warning letter to President Nixon and has long been cited by climate deniers as "proof" that global warming isn't happening.
insights.speaker: Nicolás Young
insights.so_what: This weakens a common climate-denial talking point used in policy debates.
insights.quote: I think this study actually helps show that scientists were right about a pending glaciation
